beats.narration_text: Hello. This is Liam, in for Bear. Prompt Engineering has ten multiple-answer questions, worth fifty points in total. Each contains five statements. The task is to judge each statement, not guess a pattern in the boxes.

show.event: types 'How do I guess the pattern in the multiple-answer boxes?'

props.text: How do I guess the answer pattern?

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the naive question (how to guess a pattern in the boxes) and corrects it to the real one (how to judge each statement).

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Four terms. A statement: one claim that is either true or false on its own. Checked: ticked, to say you believe the statement is true. A near-synonym: a word that means almost the same as another, but not quite. And an exact term: the one word that names a thing precisely.

terms.meaning: one claim, true or false on its own
ticked, to say you believe it is true
a word that means almost the same, but not quite
the one word that names a thing precisely

qc.sparse_reason: TERMS card: four terms, one line each.

beats.narration_text: Ten questions are worth five points each. Every question gives five statements, A to E. Judge each statement on its own. Check true statements and leave false statements unchecked. The five case questions make up the other fifty points.

shot.visual_intent: A question card; five rows A to E draw in, each a box and a line; ink checks land in three boxes; labels 'statement' and 'checked'.

show.event: the card, then rows A to E

shot.motion_claim: A question card; five rows A to E draw in, each a box and a line; ink checks land in three boxes; labels 'statement' and 'checked'.

beats.narration_text: Each statement is worth one point. So the whole question is worth five.

beats.narration_text: A statement scores its point in two cases. You checked it, and it is true. Or you left it unchecked, and it is false. In every other case, it scores zero.

shot.visual_intent: A two-by-two grid: checked / unchecked across, true / false down; coins land in checked-true and unchecked-false; ink crosses in the other two.
shot.motion_claim: A two-by-two grid: checked / unchecked across, true / false down; coins land in checked-true and unchecked-false; ink crosses in the other two.

beats.narration_text: So there is no penalty beyond the point you miss, and it is not all or nothing. Get one statement wrong, and you still keep the other four. It is five small decisions.

shot.visual_intent: Five coins in a row; an ink cross lands on one and it greys; the other four slide into the tray; a large 4.
shot.motion_claim: Five coins in a row; an ink cross lands on one and it greys; the other four slide into the tray; a large 4.

beats.narration_text: Judge each statement alone. Do not hunt for a pattern in how many are true. Any number of the five may be true. The wording and the evidence determine your decision, not the other boxes.

shot.visual_intent: Four mini cards in a row with one, two, three and four ink checks; numerals beneath; the label '1 to 4'.

beats.narration_text: The deciding phrase is inside the statement. In Prompt Engineering, being able to call a tool is not the same as being authorized to use it. Judge the actual permission and target, not a familiar technical word.

shot.visual_intent: Two sentence lines made of word slabs, identical but for one slab; the odd slab is ringed; an ink check beside the first line and a cross beside the second; 'one word'.
shot.motion_claim: Two sentence lines made of word slabs, identical but for one slab; the odd slab is ringed; an ink check beside the first line and a cross beside the second; 'one word'.

beats.narration_text: Do not use words like always or never as clues. They are not a reliable sign either way. Judge the claim, not the signal word.

beats.narration_text: For practice, try marking a printed question by hand, cold, before looking at notes or feedback. Treat each statement as a separate decision.

beats.narration_text: Then submit your attempt and read the feedback for every statement. Especially the ones you got wrong. The reasons are where the distinctions are taught.

beats.narration_text: Now, three common mistakes. One: reading the statement the way you hope it is, not the way it is written.

beats.narration_text: Two: skipping a statement because it looks familiar. A familiar word can sit inside a false claim.

beats.narration_text: Three: treating a half-true statement as true. A statement is true only if all of it is true.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. In your Prompt Engineering practice project, ask: Give me one multiple-answer question with five statements. Wait for my answer before explaining. Check every statement independently, and explain why each claim is true or false.
